content.title: HBCU, What Does It Stand For?
content.text: Written by Coursera Staff • Updated on Nov 29, 2025HBCU stands for historically Black colleges and universities, a group accounting for 3 percent of institutions in the United States. Explore the benefits of attending and the history of HBCUs. Key takeawaysHBCUs are higher education institutions founded prior to 1964 primarily to educate and enrich Black students. The US has more than 100 HBCUs, offering both undergraduate and graduate education [2].HBCU graduates have become government leaders, CEOs, and international prize winners.You can earn a degree from an HBCU to take advantage of benefits like affordability, a sense of community, and interactions with a diverse student body.Learn more about HBCUs, including their history, benefits, and notable alumni.What does HBCU stand for?HBCU stands for historically Black college and university. These schools promote a safe and diverse learning environment, allowing minority students to succeed professionally and academically. They have a powerful history of providing education, community, and social influence. HBCUs are essential higher education institutions founded to provide education and opportunities to minority students.What is an HBCU?According to the US Department of Education, an HBCU is “any historically Black college or university that was established prior to 1964” with the primary goal of educating Black Americans [3].” These schools must also have accreditation from a recognized accrediting agency. Currently, more than 100 HBCUs operate in the United States, offering undergraduate and graduate degrees [2]. About 89 percent of all HBCU campuses are in southern states [4].US News & World Report ranks Howard University in Washington, DC, as one of the best schools in the country [5] and has awarded the most PhD degrees to African American students compared to other universities. Atlanta’s Spelman College earned a spot as one of the top liberal arts colleges in the US. Take a look at other notable HBCUs:Cheyney University: This school in Pennsylvania opened in 1837, making it the nation’s first HBCU.Morehouse College: Atlanta’s all-male school has more Rhodes Scholar alums than any other HBCU. Tuskegee University: One of Alabama’s best-known HBCUs, this school is home to the Tuskegee Institute National Historic Site.Xavier University of Louisiana: This is the only historically Black Catholic university in the country. The school’s founder received the honor of canonization as a saint in 2000.History of HBCUsThe history of HBCUs dates back to before the Civil War, when Cheyney (1837), Lincoln (1854), and Wilberforce (1856) opened their doors to students. Most of the HBCUs in operation today were founded between 1865 and 1900 as an extension of the work of the American Missionary Association and the Freedman’s Bureau. In 1890, the Second Morrill Act gave states land to establish land-grant schools and ensure Black students had equal access to higher education. Florida A&M, Alabama A&M, South Carolina State University, and West Virginia State University are among the 19 land-grant universities made possible through the law.What is the #1 HBCU in America?Spelman College tops US News & World Report’s list of HBCUs, with Howard University, Morehouse College, Tuskegee University, and Florida A&M University rounding out the top five [6].Benefits of attending historically Black colleges and universitiesOne of the many advantages of attending an HBCU is affordability. You can receive a quality education for around one-third the cost of similar schools. However, students choose HBCUs for various reasons, including the following benefits.CostThe tuition at HBCUs tends to be more affordable than at non-HBCU schools, which means you can get a quality education at a fraction of the cost. UNCF estimates that the costs of attending HBCUs are around 28 percent lower than non-HBCU institutions [1]. In addition to lower tuition and fees, these schools also provide significant financial aid packages and grants to students as part of their mission to give underrepresented minority students access to higher education. Your financial aid package can include scholarships, grants, and subsidies for books, school supplies, transportation, and more.Read more: What Does FAFSA Stand For? And How to ApplyEarn Your DegreeYou are Currently on slide 1CommunityCommunity is at the heart of HBCU campuses, and they provide an inclusive experience for students of all racial and socioeconomic backgrounds grounded in the belief that anyone who wants to go to college should be able to attend. The campuses are vibrant, and students have the freedom to celebrate and share their backgrounds. Faculty and staff support students as they pursue their education, and you can develop strong relationships with your professors and classmates.CultureOne of the unique cultural benefits of attending an HBCU is the opportunity to deeply immerse yourself in Black history and culture, fostering a strong sense of identity and belonging. You also enjoy interactions with a diverse community from various African diaspora backgrounds, which enhances this rich, inclusive environment. Students at HBCUs experience a living legacy of historical significance and cultural pride, creating a supportive atmosphere where those around them celebrate Black culture daily.NetworkingThe supportive environment you encounter on an HBCU campus extends beyond graduation through the unique networking opportunities you enjoy as an alumnus. HBCUs have impressive alumni associations that allow you to connect with other graduates as you enter the workforce. The people you meet during college can become lifelong friends, and you never know when a fellow alum will be able to assist you in your career and other endeavors. Who can attend HBCUs?Anyone who meets admission requirements can attend an HBCU. Although the principal goal of HBCUs was to create a refuge and safe space to educate Black students, the demographics of the student bodies have evolved. In 2022, nearly one-fourth of the students attending HBCUs were non-Black, an increase from 15 percent in 1976 [7]. Three HBCUs are single-gender campuses. Morehouse is an all-men’s school in Atlanta. North Carolina’s Bennett College and Atlanta’s Spelman College are all-women’s schools. Notable HBCU alumniHBCU graduates have become government leaders, CEOs, and international prize winners. Some notable alumni from various HBCUs include:W.E.B.
